usage: 바뀌다 = something gets switched/replaced by something else. The thing that changes takes 이/가, never 을/를.
The traffic light changed to green.
Use ~(으)로 바뀌다 for 'change INTO': 초록불로, 다른 걸로, 평일로 — the (으)로 marks the new state.
바뀌다 also = two things get switched/mixed up: 신발이 바뀌었어요 = our shoes got switched by mistake.
Common at work/banks when a different person takes over a role — 담당자가/사장님이 바뀌다.
examples: 회의 시간이 3시로 바뀌었어요.
The meeting time got changed to 3 o'clock.
Super common at work — schedules and times 'get changed' on you; note 3시로 with (으)로.
가게 이름이 바뀌었네요.
Oh, the shop's name changed.
~네요 adds a 'huh, I just noticed' tone — natural the moment you spot a change.
계획이 또 바뀔 수도 있어요.
The plan might change again.
또 (again) + 바뀌다 is the everyday way to warn that things aren't fixed yet.
nuance: 바뀌다 is the intransitive twin of 바꾸다: the thing that changes is itself the subject (이/가) and nobody is named as the doer, so it covers things getting switched, replaced, or mixed up on their own. The dividing line vs 변하다 is key — 변하다 means a thing's inner nature transforms (사람이 변했다 = he's become a different person), while 바뀌다 means one item is swapped out for another (번호가 바뀌었다 = the number was replaced). Use 바꾸다 when YOU actively swap something (번호를 바꿨어요) and 바뀌다 when it simply ends up different (번호가 바뀌었어요). The 요-form is 바뀌어요 because the stem ends in the vowel 위, which won't contract — so spelling matters: it's 바뀌-, and the polite past is 바뀌었어요, never the wrong 바껴요/바꼈어요 that English speakers reach for by analogy.

Don't write the polite form as 바껴요 or the past as 바꼈어요; the 바뀌- stem keeps its 위 and gives 바뀌어요 / 바뀌었어요.
Don't blur 바뀌다 and 변하다: 마음이 바뀌었어요 = I changed my mind (switched decisions), but 마음이 변했어요 = my feelings have transformed (e.g., fallen out of love).

usage: 달라지다 = end up noticeably different from before. Built from 다르다 (be different) + -아지다.
뭐가 달라졌어요? is the natural way to ask 'what's different?' about a haircut, a room, a face.
Said about someone's attitude or vibe shifting for the better (or worse) — often a compliment.
안 + 달라지다 with 하나도/전혀 = 'not at all'; a warm way to tell an old friend they look the same.
examples: 머리 잘랐어요? 느낌이 달라졌네요.
Did you cut your hair? You look different.
Great compliment-ish line — 느낌이 달라지다 = the vibe/impression changed.
살아 보니까 생각이 많이 달라졌어요.
Now that I've lived here, my thinking has changed a lot.
Use for gradual inner change — 생각이/가치관이 달라지다.
내년부터 규정이 달라질 거예요.
The rules will be different starting next year.
Common in notices about policies, fees, or schedules changing.
nuance: 달라지다 spotlights the before-and-after gap: something is now clearly unlike how it used to be, which makes it the everyday verb for noticing change in a person's looks, mood, or a situation. It's the inchoative of the adjective 다르다 (to be different) — 다르 + -아지다 'become' — and that origin is the #1 pitfall: 다르다 states a static difference between two things (A는 B와 달라요 = A is different from B), while 달라지다 is the dynamic act of becoming different over time (분위기가 달라졌어요 = the mood changed). It overlaps with 변하다 and 바뀌다, but the dividing line is focus: 달라지다 = 'the result looks different now,' 변하다 = 'the inner nature transformed,' 바뀌다 = 'one thing got swapped for another.' Both 달라지다 and the thing changing take 이/가; the form 달라져요 comes from -지다 verbs taking 어 in the 요-form (지+어 → 져).

It's intransitive, so don't attach 을/를: say 생각이 달라졌어요, not 생각을 달라졌어요. To deliberately change something, use 바꾸다.
Don't say the present as 달라요 when you mean 'is changing'; 달라요 = 'is different (now)', 달라지고 있어요 = 'is becoming different'.

english: to increase, to grow, to stretch out
usage: My workload has grown a lot lately.
늘어나다 = an amount/number gets bigger. A touch more vivid and visual than plain 늘다.
The T-shirt stretched out after I washed it.
Also the everyday word for clothes losing shape — 옷이 늘어나다 (the 옷 still takes 이/가).
인구가/숫자가 늘어나다 for counts climbing; pairs naturally with 빠르게/점점/계속.
My debt keeps piling up, so I'm worried.
Money trouble: 빚이/지출이 늘어나다. 자꾸 = 'keeps (annoyingly)' increasing.
examples: 외국인 주민이 점점 늘어나고 있어요.
The foreign-resident population keeps growing.
점점 + 늘어나고 있어요 = 'is gradually increasing' — common in news and small talk.
카드값이 갑자기 늘어났어요.
My card bill suddenly went up.
Money talk: 지출이/요금이 늘어나다 (expenses/fees increase).
연습하면 단어가 자연스럽게 늘어날 거예요.
If you practice, your vocabulary will naturally grow.
Encouraging line about skills/knowledge increasing.
nuance: 늘어나다 means a quantity, number, or length gets bigger, and it feels more concrete and visual than its plainer synonym 늘다 — picture something physically stretching or a count climbing on a screen. The contrast worth memorizing: 늘다 vs 늘어나다 are near-interchangeable for amounts, but only 늘어나다 carries the physical 'stretch out and lose shape' meaning (니트가 늘어났어요), while only 늘다 is used for a skill improving (실력이 늘다, not 늘어나다). It's intransitive — the growing thing takes 이/가 — so if YOU increase something on purpose you must switch to the transitive 늘리다 (시간을 늘리다 = extend the time). The big English-speaker trap is treating 'increase' as transitive: 'I increased my savings' is 저축을 늘렸어요 with 늘리다, but 'my savings increased' is 저축이 늘어났어요.

english: to decrease, to shrink, to dwindle
usage: My stress has gone down a lot.
줄어들다 = an amount/pressure gets smaller. More vivid and gradual-feeling than plain 줄다.
My account balance is dropping fast.
인구가/회원이 줄어들다 for counts falling; the opposite of 늘어나다.
The burden has eased quite a bit.
부담이 줄어들다 = the (mental/financial) load lightens. 한결 = 'noticeably' lighter.
examples: 손님이 갑자기 줄어들었어요.
Customers suddenly dropped off.
Business small talk — 손님이/매출이 줄어들다.
체중이 조금씩 줄어들고 있어요.
My weight is gradually going down.
조금씩 + 줄어들고 있어요 = 'is decreasing little by little'.
월세 싼 데로 옮기면 부담이 줄어들 거예요.
If you move somewhere with cheaper rent, the burden will lessen.
옮기다 takes the place (데로), and 부담이 is what 줄어들다 acts on.
nuance: 줄어들다 means a quantity, size, or pressure shrinks, and it feels more vivid and gradual than its plainer synonym 줄다 — you can almost watch the number sliding down. It's the exact opposite of 늘어나다, and like that verb it pairs naturally with 점점/계속/조금씩 for a 'bit by bit' feel. Crucially it's a ㄹ-irregular (ㄹ-탈락) stem: the final ㄹ of 들- drops before the ㅂ of -ㅂ니다 and before -(으) endings, giving 줄어듭니다 and 줄어드세요 — but it stays before vowel endings, so the 요-form is 줄어들어요 and the past is 줄어들었어요. It's intransitive, the shrinking thing taking 이/가; when YOU reduce something on purpose, switch to the transitive 줄이다 (소리를 줄이다 = turn the volume down, 양을 줄이다 = cut the portion). The classic English trap is using one word for both: 비용이 줄어들었어요 = the cost went down, but 비용을 줄였어요 = I cut the cost.

usage: 사라지다 = something is gone / no longer there. The lost thing takes 이/가.
거짓말처럼 사라지다 ('vanish like a lie') is a vivid set phrase for symptoms easing fast.
Abstract feelings can 사라지다 too: 걱정이/불안이 사라지다. 서서히 = gradually fading.
examples: 눈앞에서 갑자기 사라졌어요.
It vanished right before my eyes.
눈앞에서 사라지다 = vanish from sight; 갑자기 emphasizes the suddenness.
그 카페는 1년 만에 사라졌어요.
That cafe was gone within a year.
Used for shops/places closing down and vanishing from the neighborhood; 1년 만에 = in just a year.
걱정이 곧 사라질 거예요.
Your worries will soon disappear.
Comforting line — pairs an abstract subject (걱정) with the future 사라질 거예요.
nuance: 사라지다 means something stops being present — it's gone from sight or from existence — and it works for objects, people, places, and even feelings like worry or pain. The synonym to weigh it against is 없어지다: both mean 'become gone,' but 사라지다 is more dramatic and visual, implying a clean, often sudden vanishing (지갑이 사라졌어요 = it mysteriously vanished), whereas 없어지다 is plainer and often just means 'ran out / ceased to exist' (돈이 없어졌어요 = the money's gone). It's strictly intransitive — there's no one 'doing' the disappearing, so the vanished thing is the subject (이/가). The form 사라져요 follows the -지다 pattern (지 + 어 → 져). The English trap is the transitive 'make it disappear': Korean has no transitive 사라지다, so you must use 없애다 (get rid of) or 지우다 (erase/delete) instead.

Don't default to 사라지다 for 'I ran out of X'; that's usually 없어지다 or 떨어지다: 우유가 떨어졌어요 (we're out of milk).
Don't confuse 사라지다 (to vanish) with 사다 (to buy); they only share the first syllable.

english: to come up, to arise, to form, to get
usage: 일이 생기다 = an errand/issue comes up — the #1 polite excuse for canceling plans.
A convenience store opened near my place.
생기다 = come into existence / appear, used when a new shop or building shows up.
Contact me when you get some free time.
시간이 생기다 = to get/free up time. Note 시간이, not 시간을 — English 'get' is intransitive here.
I came into a bit of money.
돈이 생기다 = money comes your way (a bonus, a refund) — you don't 'do' it, it just appears.
examples: 여드름이 또 생겼어요.
I got another pimple.
For skin/body marks: 여드름이/멍이 생기다 ('a pimple/bruise forms').
남자친구 생겼어요?
Did you get a boyfriend?
Casual but super common — 애인이/여자친구가 생기다 = 'to get a partner'.
문제가 생기면 바로 연락 주세요.
If a problem comes up, contact me right away.
문제가 생기다 = a problem arises; the conditional 생기면 is everyday phrasing.
nuance: 생기다 covers a surprisingly wide range tied by one idea — something comes into being on its own: a thing appearing (가게가 생기다), an event or issue arising (일이/문제가 생기다), or a person 'getting' something they didn't have (돈이/시간이/애인이 생기다). The crucial pitfall for English speakers is that even when English says 'get,' 생기다 is intransitive, so what you acquire takes 이/가, not 을/를: 시간이 생겼어요, never 시간을 생겼어요. Contrast it with two relatives: 생기다 = something newly comes to exist, while 만들어지다 = something gets made/created by a process, and 받다 = you actively receive something handed to you (선물을 받다, with 을/를). Note too the unrelated second sense 'to look (a certain way)': 잘생기다 = good-looking, 못생기다 = plain — here 생기다 describes appearance, not appearance-into-existence.

When canceling, '일이 생겼어요' is the natural set excuse; learners over-explain instead of using it.
Don't say 만들어요 when something just appears — 새 카페가 생겼어요 (a new cafe popped up), not 만들었어요 (which means somebody built it).

english: to break down, to get ruined
usage: My umbrella got wrecked by the wind.
망가지다 = something breaks and stops working / loses its shape. The broken thing takes 이/가; 바람에 = 'by the wind'.
For appliances/gadgets failing; close to 고장나다 but often implies real physical damage.
For cheaply-made things falling apart fast; 금방 = 'in no time'.
Rest before your health falls apart.
Figurative — 건강이/몸이 망가지다 = one's health/body gets wrecked.
examples: 택배 상자가 다 망가진 채로 왔어요.
The parcel box arrived completely wrecked.
~ㄴ 채로 = 'in a (ruined) state'; handy for complaints to delivery/sellers.
비 맞아서 신발이 망가졌어요.
My shoes got ruined from the rain.
Everyday for clothes/shoes/bags getting damaged beyond use; 비(를) 맞다 = to get rained on.
다이어트 계획이 완전히 망가졌어요.
My diet plan totally fell apart.
Figurative — plans, routines, or moods can 망가지다 ('get wrecked').
nuance: 망가지다 means something is damaged to the point it no longer works or holds its shape, and it's broader than its near-synonym 고장나다 — that word is specifically about machines/devices ceasing to function (시계가 고장났어요), whereas 망가지다 adds the nuance of physical wreckage and also stretches to objects, plans, health, and routines falling apart. So a phone that simply won't turn on is more naturally 고장났어요, but a phone with a smashed body is 망가졌어요. It's intransitive (the thing breaking takes 이/가); when a person ruins something on purpose or through carelessness, switch to the transitive 망가뜨리다 or the blunter 망치다 (계획을 망쳤어요 = I ruined the plan). The form 망가져요 follows the -지다 vowel rule (지 + 어 → 져). English speakers often try to say 'I broke it' with this verb — but you must use the transitive partner instead.

For a pure machine malfunction with no visible damage, 고장났어요 is more natural; reserve 망가지다 for real wreckage or 'falling apart'.
Don't use 망가지다 for brittle things shattering — a cup that smashes is 깨졌어요, not 망가졌어요.

english: to collapse, to crumble, to fall apart
usage: 무너지다 = a structure caves in / crumbles down. The thing that collapses takes 이/가.
멘탈이 무너지다 is super common slang among 20–30s for 'I lost it / broke down'.
My plans collapsed in an instant.
My heart sank at that news.
마음이 무너지다 = to be emotionally crushed; strong and a touch literary.
examples: 폭우로 다리가 무너졌어요.
The bridge collapsed in the heavy rain.
Disaster/news context — 건물이/다리가 무너지다; 폭우로 = 'due to torrential rain'.
한 번 졌다고 무너지지 마세요.
Don't fall apart just because you lost once.
무너지지 마세요 = 'don't break down'; encouraging someone to stay strong.
믿음이 한순간에 무너졌어요.
The trust collapsed in a single moment.
믿음이 무너지다 = trust crumbles; abstract things collapse too.
nuance: 무너지다 literally means a structure crumbles or caves in — a wall, a building, a bridge — but it's used just as often figuratively for emotions, plans, trust, or order collapsing, and among younger Koreans 멘탈이 무너지다 ('my mental collapsed') is everyday slang for breaking down under stress. The synonym to distinguish is 쓰러지다: both involve 'falling,' but 쓰러지다 means a person or upright thing topples over while staying intact (할머니가 쓰러지셨어요 = grandma collapsed/fainted), whereas 무너지다 means the thing breaks apart as it goes down. It's intransitive (the collapsing thing takes 이/가); to knock something down on purpose, use the transitive 무너뜨리다 (벽을 무너뜨리다). The 요-form is 무너져요 (지 + 어 → 져). One caution: the emotional 마음이 무너지다 is reserved for genuinely crushing moments, not mild letdowns.

mistakes: Don't use it transitively — say 건물이 무너졌어요 (the building collapsed), but 건물을 무너뜨렸어요 when something/someone brought it down.
Don't swap it with 쓰러지다 — a fainting person is 쓰러졌어요, not 무너졌어요; 무너지다 implies breaking apart, not just toppling.
Don't use 마음이 무너지다 for mild disappointment; it's strong, for heartbreak-level moments. For 'a bit let down' use 실망했어요.

english: to break, to shatter, to fall through
usage: 깨지다 = a hard/brittle thing shatters or cracks. The broken thing takes 이/가.
액정이 깨지다 is the standard way to say your phone screen is broken/cracked.
Figurative — 약속이/계약이 깨지다 = a promise/deal falls apart.
The two of them broke up in the end.
Casual slang — 깨지다 = (a couple) breaks up, like 헤어지다.
examples: 계란이 가방 안에서 깨졌어요.
The eggs broke inside my bag.
For brittle things — 유리가/접시가/계란이 깨지다.
세계 기록이 깨졌어요.
The world record was broken.
기록이 깨지다 = a record gets broken; a fixed sports/news collocation.
분위기가 갑자기 깨졌어요.
The mood was suddenly ruined.
분위기가 깨지다 = the vibe/mood breaks — when one comment spoils the moment.
nuance: 깨지다 is the verb for hard, brittle things shattering or cracking — glass, dishes, phone screens, eggs — and the key is matching the verb to the material: it contrasts with 부러지다 (long, rigid things snapping: 팔이/연필이 부러지다) and 찢어지다 (paper or fabric tearing: 종이가/옷이 찢어지다). Figuratively it covers promises, deals, records, and moods 'breaking' (약속이/기록이/분위기가 깨지다), and in casual speech 둘이 깨졌어 means a couple split up. It's intransitive (the broken thing takes 이/가); to smash something yourself, use the transitive 깨다 (컵을 깼어요 = I broke the cup) — note the e/ae spelling difference, 깨다 vs 깨지다. The 요-form is 깨져요 (지 + 어 → 져). English speakers habitually say 'I broke the glass' with the intransitive form; you must use 깨다 when there's an agent.

Match the verb to the material: glass/ceramics 깨지다, sticks/bones 부러지다, paper/clothes 찢어지다.
Don't confuse the spellings — 깨다 (transitive, 'break/smash') vs 깨지다 (intransitive, 'get broken'); the 지 marks the passive-ish 'happens to it' meaning.

english: to burst, to explode, to go off
usage: 터지다 = (signal) comes through. 와이파이/인터넷/데이터가 터지다 is the everyday way to say a signal works.
The balloon popped with a bang.
Core meaning: something bursts/explodes. 펑 is the popping sound effect.
I held it in but my anger finally exploded.
화가 터지다 = anger erupts; also 웃음이/울음이 터지다 = burst out laughing/crying.
사건이/뉴스가 터지다 = an incident/scandal breaks out; very common in media talk.
examples: 여기 지하라서 폰이 안 터져요.
It's a basement, so my phone has no signal.
폰이 안 터지다 = 'no reception' — essential for cafes, subways, basements.
물집이 터져서 아파요.
My blister popped and it hurts.
For body stuff — 물집이/혈관이 터지다.
갑자기 웃음이 터졌어요.
I suddenly burst out laughing.
웃음이 터지다 = laughter erupts; you can't hold it in — a fixed, very natural phrase.
nuance: 터지다 literally means to burst or explode — balloons, blisters, pipes, fireworks — but two everyday uses dominate life in Korea and trip up learners. First, signal coverage: 와이파이/폰이 터지다 means the signal works, and crucially 안 터져요 = 'no reception' (not 'it doesn't explode'!). Second, emotions and events erupting: 화가/웃음이/울음이 터지다 (anger/laughter/tears burst out), and 사건이 터지다 (a scandal breaks). Compare it with the milder 깨지다 (brittle things crack) — 터지다 implies internal pressure blowing outward, while 깨지다 implies a fracture from impact. It's intransitive (the bursting thing takes 이/가); to set something off or pop it yourself, use the transitive 터뜨리다 (풍선을 터뜨리다). The 요-form is 터져요 (지 + 어 → 져).

Don't translate 'burst out laughing' literally with 웃다; the idiom is 웃음이 터졌어요 (laughter burst out), with 웃음 as the subject.

usage: 멎다 = a flowing/ongoing natural thing ceases on its own. The thing that stops takes 이/가.
The wind died down for a moment.
바람이 멎다 = the wind stills; 잠시 = 'for a brief while'.
I felt like my breath stopped.
숨이/심장이 멎다 = breath/heart stops; used for shock or breathtaking moments.
examples: 눈이 멎으면 나갈게요.
I'll head out once the snow stops.
Conditional 멎으면 = 'once it stops' — natural for weather; note 멎으면 takes the 으 linker after the ㅈ-batchim.
놀라서 심장이 멎는 줄 알았어요.
I was so startled my heart felt like it stopped.
심장이 멎다 = heart stops; the set phrase 멎는 줄 알았어요 = 'I thought it would stop'.
한참 뒤에야 빗소리가 멎었어요.
The sound of rain stopped only after a long while.
Slightly literary; 멎다 has a quieter, more natural feel than 멈추다.
nuance: 멎다 means something flowing or continuous comes to a halt by itself — rain, snow, wind, bleeding, a heartbeat, breath. It overlaps with the much more common 멈추다 (to stop), but the dividing line is scope and tone: 멈추다 is the general word and works for machines, cars, and people stopping (차가 멈췄어요, 발걸음을 멈췄어요), while 멎다 is narrower, quieter, and a touch literary, reserved for natural or bodily processes ceasing on their own. So rain can be either 멎다 or 멈추다, but a car can only 멈추다, never 멎다. It's strictly intransitive and never takes an object; for stopping a vehicle or machine yourself you'd use 멈추다 or 세우다 (차를 세우다). One pronunciation note: the ㅈ-batchim means vowel endings add the 으/어 linker — hence 멎어요, 멎으면, 멎을 거예요.

It's intransitive, so don't add 을/를: 피가 멎었어요 (the bleeding stopped), not 피를 멎었어요. To stop something yourself, use 멈추다/세우다.
Don't drop the linking vowel — it's 멎으면 / 멎을 거예요 (with 으 after the ㅈ batchim), not 멎면 / 멎ㄹ 거예요.

english: to continue, to be connected, to lead to
usage: This road leads to the market.
이어지다 = one thing connects/continues to another. Often with ~(으)로 (leads to) or ~까지 (continues until).
Use for things that continue unbroken — 분위기가/대화가/날씨가 이어지다.
Small habits lead to big change.
~(으)로 이어지다 = 'leads to (a result)'; great for advice and motivation.
The tradition was passed down to descendants.
이어지다 = be handed down/carried on; 잇다's intransitive partner for legacies.
examples: 더위가 다음 주까지 이어질 거예요.
The heat will continue into next week.
Weather forecasts love this — 폭염이/장마가 이어지다; ~까지 marks how long it runs.
회의가 저녁까지 이어졌어요.
The meeting dragged on until evening.
이어지다 = an event runs on longer than expected, without stopping.
사고가 큰 피해로 이어졌어요.
The accident led to major damage.
~(으)로 이어지다 for a cause leading to a (often serious) result.
nuance: 이어지다 means something continues without breaking, or one thing connects into another — a road leading somewhere (길이 ~로 이어지다), weather persisting (더위가 이어지다), a conversation flowing on, or a cause leading to a result (X로 이어지다). It's the intransitive partner of 잇다 (to connect/join), so when you actively link things you switch to 잇다 or the compound 이어 가다 (전통을 이어 가다 = to carry on a tradition). The synonym to weigh is 계속되다 (to continue): the two overlap for duration (회의가 이어지다/계속되다 are both fine), but only 이어지다 carries the spatial 'connects to / leads to' sense — a road 이어지다 to a place, never 계속되다 there. The connected thing takes 이/가, and for 'leads to a result' the new state takes (으)로, not 에. The 요-form is 이어져요 (지 + 어 → 져).

Don't swap it with 계속되다 for spatial connection — a road that runs to the station is 역으로 이어져요, not 계속돼요.
